label: type-and-initialization-choice
name: Signed type for a never-negative quantity, uninitialized aggregate local, mutable global constant, or inconsistent or redundant member initialization
description: What breaks: implicit conversions and undefined reads. expected_blocks, res_per_block, res_bytes_per_block, pad_bytes declared int/int64_t while never negative and while callers pass uint64_t (3430026641 'Wouldn't uint make more sense', 3437522787, 3437526764, 3437527579 as suggestion blocks); dma_xfer_state locals with no initializer (2789725609, 2789768975: Wade suggested = {0}, then conceded the struct has default member initializers); file-scope MWAIT_C0 as mutable uint32_t (2380221355); praise for default member initializers followed by the question what the project standard is (2941290531); explicit = 0 initializers that value-initialization already gives (4125818552 'a bit pedantic'). Procedure: for every added local, parameter or member whose name denotes a count, size, index or byte length check the type is unsigned and matches every caller's type; for every added aggregate local without an initializer read the struct for default member initializers before suggesting = {}; for every file-scope UPPER_CASE variable require const/constexpr unless written later; for whole-file initializer sweeps cite the value-initialization rule. He asks whether an 'official guideline' exists (2789768975, 2941290531) rather than citing one; the C++ guide answer belongs in the skill prose.
disposition_reason: No existing check reads declaration types or initializers; 9 rows over 5 PRs, static.
agent_feasibility: yes: name-pattern plus type scan of added declarations, caller type comparison, struct default-initializer lookup; fully static.

members.concern: The three local counters expected_blocks, res_per_block and res_bytes_per_block (block and result-word counts for one FPGA request) plus pad_bytes are declared as signed int / int64_t although they can never be negative, so Wade asks whether an unsigned type is the right one.

detection.trigger: The diff adds or keeps a local variable, parameter or struct member of signed type (int, int64_t, long) whose name denotes a count, size, index or byte length (suffixes/words: count, cnt, blocks, bytes, size, per_block, idx, num_).
detection.procedure: For each such declaration, read every assignment and every producer function: if the producers' out-parameters or return types are unsigned (grep the file for 'uint64_t& <name>' or the callee's signature), and no code path assigns a negative value or compares against < 0, the signed type is a narrowing/sign mismatch. Also check the consumer struct field type (here rxinfo::results_per_block) with grep over h/ and src/.
detection.question: Can this variable ever legitimately hold a negative value, and do its producers and consumers already use an unsigned type?

members.quote: these 3 variables below are never expected to be negative right? Wouldn't `uint` make more sense for those? Same for `pad_bytes`?
members.note: At commit 40e4cea98609 (the review's commit) worker.cpp:1693-1696 read 'int expected_blocks = 0; int res_per_block = 0; int res_bytes_per_block = 0; int64_t pad_bytes = 0;' while the producer out-params at :566-568 were already 'uint64_t&'. The digest shows the comment against head 17c6e0117d where these are uint64_t (:1695-1698), so the author applied it. 'uint' means unsigned type in general, the fix used uint64_t. The author applied it to the locals but left three helper parameters signed, which produced the three suggestion-block comments the next day.

members.concern: The new helper fill_rxinfo (fills the rxinfo ring entry the RX worker drains) takes res_per_block as int while the caller's value is uint64_t; Wade suggests uint64_t.

detection.trigger: A new or changed function parameter has a signed integer type while every caller passes a variable of an unsigned (wider) type, or the earlier review already asked to make the same quantity unsigned.
detection.procedure: For each parameter of a new helper, grep the file for its callers and compare the argument's declared type (here the locals made uint64_t after comment 3430026641). A signed-narrower parameter receiving an unsigned-wider argument is an implicit narrowing conversion. When a prior review comment asked for unsigned on the same name, check every remaining declaration of that name in the diff (grep -n 'int res_per_block\|int res_bytes_per_block\|int64_t pad_bytes').
detection.question: Does this parameter's type match the type of the variable every caller passes, and was the same quantity already asked to be unsigned elsewhere in the PR?

members.note: Follow-up to 3430026641: the author changed the locals but not the helper signatures. At c68ea87f48 worker.cpp:1481 'int res_per_block' is passed uint64_t res_per_block from :1697-area locals and stored to rx_entry.results_per_block. Applied at head: :1482 'uint64_t res_per_block,'. Suggestion-block with no prose at all; Wade uses the GitHub suggestion feature to pin the exact one-line fix.

members.concern: The new helper write_rx_descriptors (writes RX DMA descriptors from FPGA result memory to host buffers) takes res_bytes_per_block as int while the caller passes uint64_t; Wade suggests uint64_t.

detection.trigger: A new or changed function parameter has a signed integer type while every caller passes a variable of an unsigned (wider) type, or the earlier review already asked to make the same quantity unsigned.
detection.procedure: Same as 3437522787: grep callers, compare argument type with parameter type; check the parameter is used in address arithmetic cast to uint64_t ((uint64_t)(res_bytes_per_block * block) at :1520), which is a sign of a mismatched type.
detection.question: Does this parameter's type match the type every caller passes, and is it used in unsigned address arithmetic with a cast?

members.note: At c68ea87f48 :1507 'int res_bytes_per_block,' and :1520/:1525 cast '(uint64_t)(res_bytes_per_block * block)'. Applied at head: :1507 'uint64_t res_bytes_per_block,'. Note compute_block_layout at :1097 already took uint64_t for the same name in the same commit, so the PR was internally inconsistent.

members.concern: write_rx_descriptors takes pad_bytes (bytes in the partial last result block) as int64_t while the caller passes uint64_t; Wade suggests uint64_t.

detection.trigger: A new or changed function parameter has a signed integer type while every caller passes a variable of an unsigned (wider) type, or the earlier review already asked to make the same quantity unsigned.
detection.procedure: Same as 3437522787; additionally check the sibling helper in the same diff (compute_block_layout :1098 takes 'uint64_t pad_bytes') for the type the PR itself chose for the same quantity.
detection.question: Does this parameter's type match the type every caller and sibling helper use for the same quantity?

members.note: At c68ea87f48 :1508 'int64_t pad_bytes) {' while :1098 compute_block_layout already has 'uint64_t pad_bytes,' and the caller local is uint64_t. Applied at head :1509. Third suggestion block in a 2-minute span (16:48-16:49), each as its own single-comment review, which is why the digest lists six COMMENTED reviews with no text on 2026-06-18.

members.concern: A local variable of struct type dma_xfer_state is declared without an initializer; Wade suggests zero-initialising it with '= {0}' and asks whether that is wanted.

detection.trigger: A diff adds a local of a struct or aggregate type with no initializer ('T x;'), and the variable is assigned only inside a loop or a branch below it (so a zero-iteration path could read it unset).
detection.procedure: For each such declaration, open the struct definition at HEAD (git show HEAD:path) and check whether every member carries a default member initializer. If all members have one, the declaration is already value-initialised and the finding is moot; if not, check whether a later read can precede the first assignment (e.g. the assignment sits inside 'for (head = 0; head < n_kvheads ...)' and the function returns the variable after the loop).
detection.question: Can any path read this variable before it is assigned, and does the struct definition already initialise it?

members.note: Wade read only the hunk; the struct definition in h/pos/device.hpp at the same head gives every member a default initializer (queue = nullptr, end_desc = 0, end_wrap_count = 0, readback_addr = 0, readback_value = 0), so 'dma_xfer_state xfer_state;' is already default-initialised. The author said so; Wade conceded in reply 2790148917. An agent must read the struct before raising this.

members.concern: Same zero-initialisation suggestion for another dma_xfer_state local, plus a process question: the code base is inconsistent about initialising variables and Wade asks whether an official guideline exists.

detection.trigger: Same as the sibling: an added uninitialised local of aggregate type. The second half fires when the reviewer notices the same style question twice in one PR and has no repository rule to cite.
detection.procedure: Read the struct definition for default member initializers (see 2789725609). For the guideline half, grep the repository's coding guide (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, doc/*.md) for 'initializ' and quote the rule if any; if none, the finding is an ask for a guideline, not a code change.
detection.question: Does the struct already initialise its members, and does the repository state a rule for variable initialisation?

members.quote: ... we're pretty inconsistent with variable initialization in our code. Do we have an official guideline for that?
members.note: The author answered that the standard is to initialise in the struct definition, which the head does. The '= {0}' was not applied (head line 631 'dma_xfer_state xfer;'). Wade's guideline question got no further answer in the digest.

members.concern: A new file-scope global MWAIT_C0 (the mwaitx C-state operand, 0xF << 4) is declared as a mutable uint32_t; Wade suggests making it const unless the value is meant to change at runtime.

detection.trigger: A hunk adds a namespace-scope or file-scope variable with an uppercase constant-style name, initialised from a literal expression, without const, constexpr or inline constexpr.
detection.procedure: grep the file and its includers for every write to the name (assignment, address taken, passed by non-const reference); if the only uses are reads, propose `const` (or `inline constexpr` per the project's header style) as a suggestion block.
detection.question: Is the variable ever written after initialisation, and if not, why is it not const?

members.quote:
```suggestion
const uint32_t MWAIT_C0 = (0xF << 4);
```
that is... if we don't plan to ever change this value?
members.note: Code fact at 08b5f10085: `uint32_t MWAIT_C0 = (0xF << 4);` sits at namespace tron::hardware::mwaitx scope with external linkage, next to `std::atomic<int> count_calls` and `bool MWAITX_SUPPORTED = is_supported();`. Its only uses are the two `"a"(MWAIT_C0)` asm input operands in for_event_cycles and indefinitely. The hunk moved an inline `uint32_t state = (0xF << 4);` local (with comment '0xF is (state=0) - 1') to this global. PR closed unmerged; no reply.

members.concern: Praises the new default member initializers (= 0, {0}, = nullptr) on PosDevice fields and asks what the project's formal standard for member initialization is, noting it is inconsistent across modules today.

detection.trigger: A hunk adds default member initializers to some fields of a struct whose other fields (in the same struct or neighbouring structs in the file) still have none.
detection.procedure: Read the full struct at HEAD; count members with and without an initializer; grep h/ for the same pattern in sibling headers of the same layer (h/pos, h/system); check AGENTS.md or the C++ guide for a rule on member initialization.
detection.question: After this hunk, does every pointer or counter member of the touched struct have an explicit initializer, and does the repository state a rule for it?

members.quote: I like the default initializations... I'm not sure what our formal 'standard' is for this (if we have one), but it seems very inconsistent across modules/layers today.
members.note: Verified at 5e2d19d362:h/pos/device.hpp:222-229: work_req_count = 0, num_devices = 0, worker_cmd{0}, act_slots_free = nullptr, mm_in_flight = nullptr are initialized, while neighbours rx_cpu, matmul_id, mm_cmd_fifo_depth, regions still have no initializer. mcherba replied 'we should be just standardizing on default initialization everywhere now'; the author promised a second PR to sweep the file. Not a finding against the PR; a style observation that produced follow-up work.

members.concern: Wade argues that adding explicit `= 0` / `= false` / `= nullptr` initializers to every PosDevice member is pedantic because, by the C++ value-initialization rule he cites from PR 2301, `new object()` already zero-initializes members without initializers once any default member initializer exists; he approves anyway because being explicit is good.

detection.trigger: A PR adds a mechanical, whole-file safety change (explicit initializers, redundant qualifiers, duplicated checks) whose stated reason is a guarantee the language or an existing declaration already provides.
detection.procedure: Read the PR body's stated reason (here: 'standardizing on default initialization everywhere ... better to be explicit' from PR 2193). Find how objects of the type are created (`new PosDevice(`, braces, constructor) and whether the class has a user-provided constructor (gh pr diff 2438 shows `PosDevice(int index, ...` in device.hpp). State the language rule that applies, cite the earlier PR where the team discussed it, and grade the change as redundant-but-harmless or needed.
detection.question: Does the language rule for how this type is constructed already give the guarantee the change adds, and if so is the change still wanted for explicitness?

members.quote: I think what we are doing here is a bit pedantic (in latest C++ standards, once a struct 'object' has any default member initializer, 'new object()' triggers value-initialization of the whole object, which zero-initializes all members without explicit initializers...
members.note: Full review body also says 'sorry @hvaneenoo-positron, been heads down in AoF land lately' and ends '... but I also think that being explicit is a good thing :-). Approved.' with a link to PR 2301's description. PR still open (head fc4fc8780a), no author reply in the digest. Inference, not verified: PosDevice has a user-provided constructor (`PosDevice(int index,` at device.hpp ~line 340 at head), and value-initialization of a class with a user-provided default constructor does not zero-initialize first, so the cited rule may not cover PosDevice; the explicit initializers would then be the only guarantee for members the constructor body does not set. The PR body claims the values are 'already set by constructor or init()'.

codex_bullets.bullet: Follow current repository and user conventions. Wade's naming and formatting preferences are usually nits. His later acceptance of value suffixes in established kernel code does not prescribe them for shared code.
codex_bullets.reason: Five comments (PRs 4557, 2089, 2287, 2011); naming nits are frequent (also 2982403509, 2941290531). The corpus shows Wade did raise the suffix for shared code; the Claude skill should narrow "never a finding" to the author's kernel files.
codex_bullets.claude_skill_coverage: partial (check 13 covers stems; it declares the value suffix "never a finding", which 6021333114 contradicts for shared code)
